records.name: Oman
records.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — and uniquely in the Gulf, combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveler abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, extending to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the Royal Oman Police publicly announced arresting transgender women in Salalah after private-party photos circulated on social media; HRW documented arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travelers: in February 2024, Nin Kala, an Indian non-binary model and designer arriving at Muscat airport on a tourist visa, was pulled aside while their friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. Kala warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these Gulf countries."

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Oman's criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression.

Cairo 52/White Tent joint UPR stakeholder report (Aug 2025) on trans rights in Oman: documents systemic legal and institutional discrimination - Article 266 of the Penal Code, the 'Rasd' surveillance unit monitoring and prosecuting non-conforming gender expression, prohibition of legal gender recognition and explicit ban on gender-affirming healthcare; Oman disregards prior UPR recommendations.

Cairo 52 country review of Oman: the 2018 Penal Code explicitly and implicitly criminalises trans expression and identity (Chapter 3); Royal Decree No. 75 (2019) prohibits healthcare practitioners from providing any gender-affirming care to trans people; legal gender recognition severely limited; cybercrime laws used to punish queer and trans expression.

LegalClarity overview (June 2026): Oman criminalises all same-sex conduct (Articles 261-262 of the 2018 Penal Code, up to 3 years) and restricts gender expression, with consequences extending to foreign nationals (deportation on top of prison) and digital activity; prosecution generally requires a spouse/relative complaint unless a 'public scandal' occurred - an exception that swallows the rule.

The News Minute (Feb 2023): genderqueer/non-binary model and activist Nin Kala alleges a transphobic ordeal at Muscat airport - taken to an isolated room, made to remove her shirt twice 'for examination', touched inappropriately, and told to return to India despite a valid 10-day tourist visa.

HRW letter (July 2020) to Oman's Attorney General re: arrests and convictions under the 2018 Penal Code - four men arrested after photos from a private birthday party in Salalah circulated on Snapchat, convicted of 'immoral conduct', 'imitating the opposite sex' (Art. 266(d)) and cybercrime provisions; each sentenced to 3 years, a fine and street cleaning.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Oman's criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.

Shafiqa Ahmadi, 'Islam and Homosexuality: Religious Dogma, Colonial Rule, and the Quest for Belonging' (Journal of Civil Rights and Economic Development, 2012): distinguishes homosexual acts from homosexual persons; in some Islamic countries acts are criminalised (even by death) while identity alone is not - scholarly context for Oman's legal-religious framework.

records.name: Pakistan
records.summary:
Pakistan is dangerous — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act was "one of the most progressive internationally" (third-gender recognition since 2009), but the Federal Shariat Court gutted it in 2023 (declaring provisions "un-Islamic"). Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi (bodies on a roadside), 267 violence cases were documented in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions), and there is no Sharia cross-dressing criminalisation (unlike Malaysia). No trans-traveler-specific border friction or death in custody is documented (unlike the UAE or Indonesia). But the severity of social and police violence is extreme.

Pakistan has a significant hijra/third-gender community with some legal recognition, and civil society is active (a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety launched in Lahore, and activists are appealing the Shariat Court ruling to the Supreme Court).

sources.claim: AP (Nov 2024): 'Shooting kills 3 transgender women in Pakistan's largest city' — gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

BBC (Sept 2025): the bodies of three transgender people, shot dead, were found on a roadside in Karachi's Memon Goth area - the latest violence against a community of an estimated half a million trans citizens facing social exclusion and abuse; Amnesty notes a concerning rise in violence; the 2018 Transgender Rights Act's key sections were later revoked by a sharia court.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief (April 2026): 'Preventing Torture Against Transgender Persons in Pakistan' - trans people face a continuum of violence from law enforcement (harassment, arbitrary detention, extortion, custodial abuse); the challenge is not absence of legal protections but failure of implementation - no binding operational frameworks, independent oversight or accessible complaint mechanisms.
UK Home Office CPIN Pakistan: sexual orientation and gender identity or expression (Nov 2025, updated July 2026): official country-of-origin information and assessment for asylum claims.

Amnesty International (May 2023): responding to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 - 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group'; some court observations were based on presumptive scenarios rather than empirical evidence.

The News (Oct 2025): 'Between legal rights and lived realities' - despite the 2018 Act, trans Pakistanis face violence, harassment, landlord rejection and hospital/police apathy; in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa alone 267 cases of violence over five years with only one conviction; traces the legal history from the Criminal Tribes Act 1871 through the 2011 Supreme Court recognition, the 2018 Act, the 2020 'X' marker rules, and the 2023 FSC strike-down of self-identification.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Feb 2026): anti-trans officials and violence reverse progress for transgender Pakistanis - Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposes a government 'gender re-assignment board' controlling official gender identity; a wave of violence (shootings at activists' homes) has left trans people afraid to go out; the 2023 shariat court ruling undercut the 2018 law.

Dawn (May 2023) by Nayyab Ali: 'Westernised transgenders or colonised transphobes?' - examines the FSC verdict on the Transgender Rights Act; the petitioners' concerns echo right-wing Western anti-trans narratives; describes the 2018 Act's protections (anti-discrimination, welfare, offences against trans people).

The Diplomat (July 2025): Pakistan's transgender citizens - legally recognized, socially forsaken; for 500,000 trans Pakistanis, constitutional rights remain hollow in the face of violence and exclusion.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

records.name: Panama
records.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex activity legal since 2008 (Presidential Decree 332); but same-sex marriage ruled not a constitutional human right by the Supreme Court (March 2023); no explicit SOGISC discrimination protections (amendment blocked by the National Assembly in 2024); harassment, violence and discrimination not formally recognised as hate crimes; conservative religious actors consistently oppose advances.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).
Washington Blade (Feb 2018): a Panama Supreme Court judge withdrew a draft ruling against same-sex marriage after public outcry - part of the court's long-running marriage litigation.

BBC Travel (Aug 2018): 'Guna Yala: The islands where women make the rules' - in the indigenous Guna territory off Panama, a flourishing 'third gender' community (omeggid) is celebrated, with natural gender equality and tolerance of gender fluidity - a striking cultural counterpoint to national law.

Outright International country overview for Panama (updated March 2026): same-sex conduct legal since 2008 (Presidential Decree 332); legal gender recognition possible; but no marriage or adoption, and the March 2023 Supreme Court ruling that same-sex marriage is not a constitutional human right foreclosed domestic avenues; no SOGI anti-discrimination laws (amendments blocked in 2024); police abuse of trans women reported.
Washington Blade (Oct 2017): a Panama Supreme Court judge ruled against same-sex marriage in a draft opinion - the first of the court's rulings in the marriage cases.

records.name: Pitcairn Islands
records.summary:
Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

The earlier profile's 'Christian-conservative, no public LGBT life' clause appeared in no source and has been deleted; it was the only stated basis for placing this territory below its administering state, which the legal record does not support. What the sources do say is that no islander is known to be in a same-sex relationship — on an island this size, invisibility is arithmetic rather than atmosphere, and defence is the administering state's responsibility.

sources.claim: Alchetron (Wikipedia-derived): LGBT rights in the Pitcairn Islands - same-sex activity legal since 2001; 2010 constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination; same-sex marriage since 14 May 2015 (though none of the ~50 islanders is known to be in a same-sex relationship); adoption legal since 2015.

ReadableWiki (Wikipedia-derived): LGBTQ rights in the Pitcairn Islands - marriage defined as union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity; the Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises foreign civil partnerships; adoption open to married, unmarried and single people.
WIKI2 (Wikipedia mirror): LGBT rights in the Pitcairn Islands - legal since 2001, discrimination protections since 2010, same-sex marriage and adoption since 2015; defence is UK responsibility.

records.name: Peru
records.summary:
Peru demands real caution with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence against trans people, but no criminalisation of trans identity and an unprecedented 17-year conviction for police torture of a trans woman. Congress approved (February-April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated axis-C restriction comparable to US state bans or the UK EHRC code. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 TLGBI people were assassinated (trans women most affected). In the Azul Rojas Marín case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025) — an unprecedented conviction for Peru and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. A presidential decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024), but was walked back after massive protests.

For a visitor: no border friction, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure when using public facilities.

sources.claim: Infobae (Feb 2025, in Spanish): Peru's Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a bill barring people from using public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex (bills 6506 and 8457 by Montoya and Muñante); activist Gianna Camacho called it discriminatory; also bans 'ambiguous' signage in bathrooms.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis (in Spanish): 'Discriminación legalizada' - commentary on the Peruvian Congress's prohibition of trans people accessing public bathrooms, analysing the measure as legalised discrimination.

Presentes (July 2024, in Spanish): hate crimes increased in Peru and trans women are the most affected - 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 rights violations 2020-2023 per the Cayetano Heredia University Observatory; documents the extortion-killing of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano by the 'Los Gallegos' criminal gang, with victims' bodies filmed as extortion threats.

BBC Mundo (Dec 2025): 17 years' prison for three Peruvian police officers for raping and torturing trans woman Azul Rojas Marín - the first conviction in Peru for a case of discrimination-based sexual torture, and the first Inter-American Court case recognising discrimination-motivated torture in the region (2008 case, Casa Grande).

Infobae (Dec 2025, in Spanish): the Azul Rojas aggressors receive their sentence almost 20 years later - 17 years' effective imprisonment; the first time Peruvian justice convicted state agents for prejudice-motivated sexual torture of an LGBTI person, fulfilling Inter-American Court measures (Peru publicly acknowledged responsibility and apologised in 2022).
Human Rights Watch (May 2025): 'Peru: New Law Threatens Free Speech, Trans Rights' — a crime-prevention law's vague provisions chill expression and endanger trans people's rights.

Human Rights Watch (Jun 2024): 'Peru Walks Back Anti-Trans Guidance in Health System' — health ministry reverses guidance classifying trans identities as 'mental health problems' requiring conversion-style assessment.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): one of the few South American countries not recognising same-sex couples; trans people can rectify name/gender markers only via an expensive, complicated court process taking years; a 2017 law bans SOGI discrimination but violence persists and hate crimes go unpunished; in 2024 the Health Ministry unexpectedly issued a decree classifying trans identity as a mental-health condition.

Peru Support Group (April 2025): 'A week of setbacks' - Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR banning people from using public bathrooms counter to their birth sex and banning inclusive signage; criticised by the Ombudsman's Office; part of a broader rollback of gender, LGBTQ+ and reproductive rights.

The Perchy Bird (May 2017): Peru's Congress voted 66-29 to remove LGBT terms from hate-crime legislation, repealing the section of President Kuczynski's January 2017 decree that had extended hate-crime protections to sexual orientation and gender identity after a million-signature petition; Peru returned to being one of three South American countries with no LGBT anti-discrimination laws (with Paraguay and Guyana).

records.name: Philippines
records.summary:
The Philippines is one of Asia's most socially accepting destinations for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity (bakla, tomboy), a vibrant Manila Pride, and no criminalisation. Trans identity has never been criminalised.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (trans people cannot change their gender marker), the SOGIE Equality Bill has been stalled for 25 years (no national anti-discrimination law), and documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a Chinese national arrested for raping a transwoman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The Commission on Human Rights actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction, social acceptance is genuine, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue (documented incidents of bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials).

sources.claim: Outright International (IGLHRC) country overview for the Philippines (updated March 2026): consistently ranked among Asia's most 'accepting' countries toward LGBTIQ persons; but only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions (2018 SWS) and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets; EO 100 s.2019 institutionalised the Diversity and Inclusion Program, strengthened by EO 51 s.2023; no legal gender recognition.

Bulatlat (June 2025): the killing of 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol (found in a Cagayan river days after going missing) prompts groups to push for the SOGIESC Equality Bill; Bahaghari alliance calls it another harrowing case in a series of recent trans killings.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Manila Bulletin report (May 2025) covers a foreigner arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (April 2024): the assault on drag artist Taylor Sheesh mid-performance in Bayambang, Pangasinan sparks renewed push for the SOGIE Equality Bill; the artist described the incident as traumatic.
Rolling Stone Philippines: 'Laws that LGBTQ+ Filipinos need to know' - overview of the few laws protecting LGBTQ+ Filipinos and the gaps (no national SOGIE law, no marriage equality).
Rappler: transgender Filipinos demand legal gender recognition - advocacy for the right to change identity documents.

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel safety page for Manila (2026): safety confidence scores (LGBTQ+ 69 'Generally Safe', Trans 62 'Exercise Caution'); strong social acceptance and cultural visibility (bakla/tomboy traditions, vibrant Pride) coexist with near-complete absence of national legal protections; the SOGIE Equality Bill (filed 2000) remains stuck in Congress.

HRW report (June 2017) 'Just Let Us Be': discrimination against LGBT students in the Philippines - bullying and exclusion in schools; opens with Edgar T., 18: '[Senator and boxing legend] Manny Pacquiao says we're not human. They should just let us be'; Philippine law provides protections but implementation is lacking.

records.name: Palau
records.summary: Palau demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2014; small, US-associated, tourism-dependent; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council; Palau was among Pacific countries supporting the call.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Oct 2014): Palau decriminalised homosexuality by introducing a new Penal Code with no sodomy provisions, signed by the President in April 2014 - the Attorney General confirmed the repeal; 'the benefit of legislating, rather than litigating'.

Scoop/OHCHR opinion (Oct 2011) by Matilda Bogner: 'Decriminalizing homosexuality is an essential first step towards establishing genuine equality before the law' - notes Pacific Island countries including Palau supported the UN call for decriminalisation and equal rights.

records.name: Papua New Guinea
records.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.

sources.claim: ADB publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in Asia and the Pacific - regional comparative overview including Papua New Guinea.
HRW (Jan 2009): 'Where Violence Against Women is Rampant' - documents widespread gender-based violence in Papua New Guinea, the context of impunity that also affects sexual and gender minorities.

ABC News (Oct 2014): 'Papua New Guinea's gay and transgender community finds safety in Hanuabada village' - the coastal village on Port Moresby's outskirts (best known for producing half the national cricket team) is a safe haven for the gay and trans community in a country where homosexuality is illegal.

The Guardian (Jan 2017): HRW says PNG has failed to respond to corruption and police violence and failed to protect women and children - a scathing assessment including Australia's offshore detention on the island.

Guardian (Nigeria) Life (Nov 2018): 'Papua New Guinea Has A Village For LGBT Community' - openly gay 24-year-old Kapera Patrick remembers thugs pelting him with abuse, stones and bottles; Hanuabada village offers refuge where gay sex is illegal and stigma and violence are widespread.
